Herd
H'RD
n. (rendering Hebrew bāqār and 'ēder, Greek agelē)
From Old English heord, a company of beasts. Hebrew distinguishes sharply between the bāqār, the herd of cattle, and the tsō'n, the flock of sheep and goats, and the King James keeps the distinction throughout — flocks and herds being the standard pairing for the whole of a pastoral man's living. To lose both was to lose everything.

Biblical Definition

The herd is the substance of a pastoral people, and Scripture uses it to measure both blessing and loss. Abram and Lot separate because the land could not carry two men's wealth: “And Lot also, which went with Abram, had flocks, and herds, and tents” (Gen 13:5) — the herd is what forces the choice that will take Lot to Sodom. Under the covenant the herd is one of the named tokens of God's favour: “he will also bless the fruit of thy womb, and the fruit of thy land, thy corn, and thy wine, and thine oil, the increase of thy kine, and the flocks of thy sheep” (Deu 7:13). Which makes the great confession of Habakkuk the more remarkable, since he deliberately strips away every one of those tokens before he states his joy: “Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls” (Hab 3:17) — and the verse that follows is yet I will rejoice in the LORD. The prophet names the empty stall and rejoices anyway, which is the whole doctrine of faith in one sentence. The herd is also the figure under which God describes His own care and His own judging, distinguishing between one beast and another within the same herd: “Therefore will I save my flock, and they shall no more be a prey; and I will judge between cattle and cattle” (Eze 34:22).

Webster 1828 Definition

A collection of beasts feeding or driven together, particularly of the larger cattle as distinguished from a flock of sheep; in Scripture the substance of a pastoral household, a token of covenant blessing, and the empty stall of Habakkuk's faith.

expand to see more

HERD, n. 1. A collection or assemblage of beasts, feeding or driven together.

2. Applied chiefly to the larger cattle, as oxen and kine; a flock being of sheep or goats.

3. A company of men, in contempt; the rabble; the vulgar herd.

4. In Scripture, flocks and herds, the whole substance of a pastoral people. Gen. 13.

5. There shall be no herd in the stalls: yet I will rejoice in the LORD. Hab. 3.

Key Scripture

Genesis 13:5 — "And Lot also, which went with Abram, had flocks, and herds, and tents."

Deuteronomy 7:13 — "And he will love thee, and bless thee, and multiply thee: he will also bless the fruit of thy womb, and the fruit of thy land, thy corn, and thy wine, and thine oil, the increase of thy kine, and the flocks of thy sheep, in the land which he sware unto thy fathers to give thee."

Habakkuk 3:17 — "Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls:"

Ezekiel 34:22 — "Therefore will I save my flock, and they shall no more be a prey; and I will judge between cattle and cattle."

Modern Corruption

Covenant blessing is converted into a guaranteed formula of material increase, so that prosperity becomes the proof of God's favour and loss the proof of His displeasure — a doctrine Habakkuk explicitly refuses.

expand to see more

Deu 7:13 and the like promises are the raw material of every prosperity doctrine: because God promised increase of kine and flocks to a covenant nation in a particular land under particular terms, it is inferred that material abundance is the standing entitlement of faith, and that the believer who lacks it must be deficient in it. Two things are wrong with the inference. The promises were made to national Israel under the Mosaic covenant, with corresponding national curses attached in the same passage; and the New Testament transposes the blessings, telling believers plainly that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God, and that all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution. The apostles were not men with full stalls, and Paul learned both how to be abased and how to abound.

Hab 3:17 is the decisive text, and it is decisive because the prophet enumerates the covenant tokens one by one and removes them: no blossom, no fruit, no oil, no meat, no flock, no herd. That is the covenant blessing catalogue read backwards, and he says yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation. He does not claim the losses will be reversed, nor argue that they are unreal; he grounds joy in the LORD Himself rather than in His gifts. The principle to recover is that God's goodness is not measured by the contents of the stall, and that a faith which requires the herd to be there has never yet been tested. The opposite error — treating poverty as itself a virtue — Scripture equally denies; the herds were a genuine blessing, given and taken by the same hand.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew bāqār is the herd of oxen, distinguished from tsō'n, the flock of sheep and goats; 'ēder is a drove or flock generally. Greek agelē is a herd, used in the Gospels of the swine at Gadara.

expand to see more

Hebrew bāqār (H1241) — herd, oxen, cattle of the larger sort; paired constantly with tsō'n to mean a man's whole living.

Hebrew tsō'n (H6629) — the flock of sheep and goats; the smaller cattle, and the figure under which God's people are most often described.

Hebrew 'ēder (H5739) — a drove, flock, or herd; used of the flocks Jacob divided and of the tower of the flock (Mic 4:8).

Hebrew miqneh (H4735) — cattle as acquired substance; Lot also... had flocks, and herds, and tents (Gen 13:5).

Greek agelē (G34) — a herd; used only of the herd of swine into which the legion was permitted to go (Mar 5:11).

Usage

"Of pastoral substance forcing a choice: Lot also, which went with Abram, had flocks, and herds, and tents (Gen 13:5)."

"Of covenant blessing: he will also bless... the increase of thy kine, and the flocks of thy sheep (Deu 7:13)."

"Of faith with the stall empty: there shall be no herd in the stalls (Hab 3:17), followed by yet I will rejoice in the LORD."
